title: Break it down
objective: Turn a problem that feels too big into small questions you can answer one at a time.

sources.title: Pólya, How to Solve It (Princeton University Press): heuristics for problem solving, including breaking a problem into parts and working backwards

simplifies: Real problems rarely split this neatly the first time. Expect to redo the split once you learn more; that is normal, not a failure.

steps.caption: The big question: is "Racecar" a palindrome (the same forwards and backwards)? Too vague to code in one go. Split it into smaller questions.
Small question 1: what exactly do we compare? Ignore upper and lower case, so "Racecar" becomes "racecar".

predict.prompt: Which small question should come first?

options.text: Decide what counts as the same letter (R and r)
options.explanation: Right. Until you settle that, every later comparison could give the wrong answer.
Not yet. Writing code before the small questions are answered usually means rewriting it.

options.text: Test it on a long sentence
options.explanation: Testing comes later. First decide what the program should even compare.

steps.caption: Small question 2: do the first and last letters match? r and r: yes.
Small question 3: then what? Move both ends one step inward and compare again: a and a, then c and c.

predict.prompt: The first and last letters match. What is the next small step?

options.explanation: Too early. One matching pair says nothing about the letters in between.

options.text: Move both ends inward and compare the next pair
options.explanation: Right. The same small check, repeated, covers the whole word.

options.text: Start again from the first letter
options.explanation: That would compare the same pair forever. Each check should move inward.

steps.caption: Small question 4: when do we stop? When the two ends meet in the middle (palindrome), or as soon as a pair doesn't match (not a palindrome).

options.text: Only after checking every letter twice
options.explanation: No need. Each pair is checked once as the ends move inward.

options.text: When the ends meet, or at the first pair that doesn't match
options.explanation: Right. Meeting in the middle means every pair matched; one mismatch is already enough to say no.
One match is not enough: a later pair could still differ.

steps.caption: Each small answer was easy. Together they solve the big question: "racecar" is a palindrome. That is decomposition.

quiz.prompt: You're asked: "Find which customers ordered more this month than last month." What's the best first move?

options.text: Start writing a loop over all customers
options.explanation: Code first usually means rework. You don't yet know what "ordered more" is measured in.

options.text: Split it: what counts as an order? how do I total a month? then compare two totals
options.explanation: Right. Each of those is a small question you can answer and test on its own.
Speed isn't the problem yet; the question isn't broken down.

quiz.prompt: A small question is a good one when…

options.text: You can answer it and check the answer on its own
options.explanation: Right. If you can test it alone, you can trust it when you combine the pieces.

options.text: It sounds as hard as the original
options.explanation: Then it isn't smaller. Keep splitting until each part is easy to answer.

options.text: It needs every other part solved first
options.explanation: That's a sign the split isn't working: good parts can mostly be solved independently.
